headline: Former Connecticut official sentenced to 7 years after fleeing to Greece
dek: Kosta Diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him.
body: Former Connecticut school-construction official Konstantinos “Kosta” Diamantis was sentenced Wednesday to 84 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release, but he was not in the Bridgeport courtroom to hear the punishment. The 70-year-old former state official had fled to Greece before sentencing, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Connecticut said law enforcement is seeking him. The federal announcement is at https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-state-official-sentenced-7-years-federal-prison-school-construction-extortion-and.

U.S. District Judge Stefan R. Underhill imposed the sentence for convictions involving extortion, bribery, conspiracy and false statements. A federal jury in Bridgeport found Diamantis guilty in October 2025 on 21 counts: two counts of extortion, two extortion-conspiracy counts, two bribery counts, two bribery-conspiracy counts and 13 counts of making false statements to federal agents, according to the Justice Department. Connecticut Public reported that the case grew out of Diamantis’s work as the state’s former deputy budget director and director of the Office of School Construction Grants and Review.

That office administered grants for Connecticut public-school construction projects seeking state funding. Prosecutors said Diamantis used the position to demand and receive payments from contractors while helping them obtain or preserve work. The Justice Department identified projects involving a school project in Tolland, state reimbursement work for New Britain and renovations at Hartford’s Bulkeley High School. The release says one contractor paid Diamantis with cash and checks and hired his daughter at an inflated salary; those details describe the conduct underlying the convictions, not new untested allegations.

The sentence came after an unusual break in the normal criminal-justice process. Diamantis had been scheduled to appear for sentencing in September but did not attend. CT Mirror reported that his lawyer told the court Diamantis had left the United States and was in Greece, where he holds dual citizenship. The later sentencing could proceed without him, but his absence leaves the practical question of how and when he will be taken into custody. Federal officials have not announced that he has returned to the United States.

The financial consequences are not settled. The Justice Department said Judge Underhill will determine restitution after additional court proceedings. That decision could identify losses that the government says were caused by the scheme, but the sentencing announcement did not give a final restitution amount. The unresolved figure matters because the projects at issue involved public school construction and state reimbursement, placing the case's consequences beyond the contractors and former official who appeared in court.

The prison term was also shorter than the range sought by prosecutors. CT Mirror reported that the government recommended a guideline range of 121 to 151 months, while the judge imposed 84 months. The difference does not change the convictions or the three-year supervised-release term, but it will be part of the record as prosecutors pursue Diamantis and the court addresses restitution. CT Mirror’s sentencing report is at https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/30/kosta-diamantis-still-a-fugitive-sentenced-to-84-months/.

The case is not finished for the other people involved in the investigation. The Justice Department said contractors identified as Duffy, Monarca and Roy pleaded guilty to related charges and are awaiting sentencing. The investigation was conducted by the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation, and federal prosecutors said the bribery scheme involved multimillion-dollar school-construction projects. Connecticut Public’s account of the sentencing, including the fact that Diamantis remained outside the country, is at https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-09-30/kosta-diamantis-cts-disgraced-former-deputy-budget-director-sentenced.

For Connecticut, the public-interest question now extends from the sentence to the systems that allowed a senior official overseeing school-building money to steer contractors while concealing conduct from investigators. The court has established criminal responsibility through the jury’s verdict and the sentence; it has not yet completed restitution proceedings or resolved Diamantis’s custody. Those next steps will determine how much money is recovered, whether the former official is returned to face the prison term and what accountability reaches the related contractors.
author: NorthEast News Desk
